title: Hasidism for everyone
hook: Buber, Heschel and Zalman Schachter-Shalomi brought Hasidic ideas to wide audiences

segments.voice: Yesterday, women of the court: rebbetzins, daughters and teachers who shaped Hasidic life from the side rooms. Did you thank someone who works behind the scenes? Day one thousand two hundred seven.

Rabbi Zusya lies on his deathbed, and he's afraid. His students are puzzled. You, afraid? He answers with a story about himself. When I come before the heavenly court, he says, they won't ask me, Zusya, why weren't you Moses? They'll ask me, Zusya, why weren't you Zusya? That little tale was told among Hasidim. Then it traveled. It turns up in sermons, classrooms and graduation speeches, far from any rebbe's table. Today's word is about how it got there.
screen: `ZUSYA, AFRAID.` → `WHY WEREN'T YOU ZUSYA?` → `THE TALE TRAVELED.`

segments.voice: Hasidism for everyone. Three teachers carried Hasidic ideas beyond the court. Turn it four ways. First, Martin Buber. He gathered Hasidic tales from old Hebrew and Yiddish books and retold them in German, then they reached English. Through him, readers who would never visit a court met Zusya and the Baal Shem Tov. Buber heard in Hasidism a teaching that God is met in the ordinary meeting between people, here, now, not somewhere far away. Second, Abraham Joshua Heschel. He came from a family of Hasidic rebbes and became a teacher and writer in America. In his book on the Sabbath, he describes Shabbat as holiness in time rather than in a place, a sanctuary built of hours. He wrote about wonder, and about a God who cares about human beings. Third, Zalman Schachter-Shalomi, usually called Reb Zalman. He was trained in Chabad, then went on to help found what became Jewish Renewal, bringing niggunim, Hasidic stories and meditative prayer into new communities. Fourth, the argument. Not everyone was pleased. Some critics, including the scholar Gershom Scholem, said Buber picked out the tales, set aside the Hasidic teachers' own written teachings, and read his own philosophy into what was left. Some Hasidim would say the court, its law and its life, is the point. Others answer that the sparks were always meant to travel. You don't have to settle it today. Notice only that Zusya's question now gets asked in rooms where no one wears a shtreimel.
screen: `BUBER RETELLS THE TALES.` · `HESCHEL: HOLINESS IN TIME.` · `REB ZALMAN AND RENEWAL.` · `NOT EVERYONE WAS PLEASED.` · then, large: `HASIDISM BEYOND THE COURT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one idea of theirs, starting with Zusya's. Settle, and breathe. Let the question come to you in your own name. Not, why weren't you someone else, someone braver or holier or more famous. Just: why weren't you you? Is there one part of yourself you've been setting aside to look like someone else? Don't scold yourself. Just notice it, and breathe with it. If you pray, you can hold the question there. The bell holds the time.
Hasidism for everyone. Buber, Heschel and Reb Zalman carried Hasidic tales and ideas to wide audiences, and people still argue about what traveled and what stayed behind. Today's word.
Your line: hasidism beyond the court. Today, when you catch yourself trying to be someone else, ask Zusya's question once. Day one thousand two hundred seven.

howItsDone: Readers meet Hasidic ideas through Buber's retold tales and Heschel's books, and in Jewish Renewal and other communities that sing niggunim and tell Hasidic stories; Hasidic courts continue their own life of study and prayer.
